topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: Sherman Act Section 2 prohibits monopolization. To establish an unlawful monopolization claim against a firm, a plaintiff must generally show possession of monopoly power in a relevant market PLUS:
choice_a: That the firm charges the lowest prices in its market
choice_b: The willful acquisition or maintenance of that power through exclusionary conduct, as opposed to growth from a superior product or business acumen
choice_c: That the firm has more than two competitors
choice_d: That the firm is a publicly traded corporation
explanation: Unlike Section 1, which requires an agreement between two or more parties, Section 2 can reach a single firm's unilateral conduct -- but only where the firm has monopoly power AND obtained or maintained it through exclusionary or predatory conduct, not merely by winning on the merits.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust); 15 U.S.C. 2 (Sherman Act Section 2)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: A local real estate board publishes a suggested or recommended commission-rate schedule for its member firms to follow. Even though membership is voluntary and the schedule is only labeled "suggested," this practice is:
choice_a: Fully protected because trade associations are exempt from antitrust law
choice_b: Legal as long as the word "suggested" appears on the schedule
choice_c: Likely to be treated as unlawful price fixing, because a trade association's recommended fee schedule can function as an anticompetitive signal that discourages independent pricing
choice_d: Only a concern if every member firm actually adopts the exact rate
explanation: Courts have repeatedly held that a trade association's published fee schedule -- even one styled as merely "recommended" or "suggested" -- can constitute unlawful price fixing because it signals a target rate and discourages independent price competition among members.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: In antitrust analysis, how are horizontal restraints among competing brokerages (such as price fixing, group boycotts, and market allocation) typically treated compared to most vertical restraints (such as a franchisor's rules for its own franchisees)?
choice_a: Both are always evaluated identically under the rule of reason
choice_b: Both are always per se illegal regardless of context
choice_c: Vertical restraints are always treated more harshly than horizontal restraints
choice_d: Horizontal restraints of this kind are usually condemned as per se illegal, while many vertical restraints are instead evaluated under the more flexible "rule of reason"
explanation: Certain horizontal agreements among competitors -- price fixing, group boycotts, market allocation -- are so consistently anticompetitive that courts condemn them per se, without inquiry into actual market effect. Many vertical restraints, by contrast, are assessed under the rule of reason, which weighs procompetitive justifications against anticompetitive effects.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: Under the intra-enterprise (or intra-corporate) conspiracy concept in antitrust law, an agreement between a single brokerage firm and its own employees or agents, acting within the scope of that one firm's business:
choice_a: Generally cannot itself form the "conspiracy" that Sherman Act Section 1 requires, because Section 1 targets concerted action between separate, competing economic actors, not one firm's internal decision-making
choice_b: Is always treated as a per se antitrust violation
choice_c: Requires DOJ approval before the firm may set its own internal commission splits
choice_d: Is illegal only if the firm has more than 50 employees
explanation: Section 1 requires concerted action between separate, independent actors. A single firm directing its own agents on matters like internal commission splits is unilateral conduct by one economic enterprise, not a conspiracy between competitors -- even though those same agents might individually hold real estate licenses.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: Following a major 2024 nationwide antitrust settlement affecting residential real estate brokerage practices, one significant industry-wide practice change was that:
choice_a: The MLS was abolished nationwide
choice_b: Offers of buyer-broker compensation could no longer be published as a field on the Multiple Listing Service, decoupling that compensation from the MLS listing itself
choice_c: All real estate commissions were set at a fixed federal rate
choice_d: Buyers were prohibited from having a buyer's agent
explanation: Among the practice changes stemming from the 2024 settlement, MLS rules were changed nationwide to remove the field for offers of buyer-broker compensation, so that such compensation is no longer published or communicated through the MLS listing itself.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust); 2024 NAR nationwide settlement practice changes

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: As part of the practice changes flowing from the 2024 nationwide real estate antitrust settlement, buyer's agents affiliated with MLS-participating firms are now generally required to:
choice_a: Charge every buyer an identical, board-set commission rate
choice_b: Refuse to work with any buyer who has not yet obtained mortgage pre-approval
choice_c: Enter into a written buyer representation agreement with a buyer before touring homes with that buyer
choice_d: Disclose their personal income to the buyer before showing any property
explanation: One of the key practice changes was a new requirement that buyer's agents have a written agreement with the buyer, entered into before touring homes, that discloses and specifies the agent's compensation -- intended to make buyer-agent compensation a matter of individual, transparent negotiation rather than a boilerplate industry practice.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust); 2024 NAR nationwide settlement practice changes

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: As a matter of basic federal antitrust principle applicable to real estate brokerage, commission rates and fees charged by any individual brokerage firm must always be:
choice_a: Set by the state real estate commission
choice_b: Identical across all firms operating in the same market
choice_c: Published in a single nationwide fee schedule
choice_d: Fully negotiable and independently set by each firm, never fixed, suggested, or standardized by an MLS, board, association, or group of competing firms
explanation: A cornerstone of federal antitrust compliance in real estate is that commissions are always negotiable and must be independently determined by each firm -- no MLS, board, association, or agreement among competitors may fix, standardize, or suggest a uniform rate.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition." Compared to the Sherman Act, the FTC Act's Section 5 standard is generally understood to be:
choice_a: Broader than the Sherman Act, allowing the FTC to reach some anticompetitive conduct in the real estate industry that might not independently satisfy every element of a Sherman Act claim
choice_b: Narrower than the Sherman Act and rarely enforceable
choice_c: Limited exclusively to conduct by real estate licensees
choice_d: Identical in every respect to Sherman Act Section 1, with no independent enforcement value
explanation: The FTC Act's "unfair methods of competition" standard under Section 5 is generally understood as broader than the Sherman Act, giving the FTC an additional enforcement tool against anticompetitive practices in industries including real estate brokerage.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust); 15 U.S.C. 45 (FTC Act Section 5)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: Criminal prosecution of a Sherman Act Section 1 price-fixing violation in the real estate industry is most directly the responsibility of:
choice_a: The state real estate licensing board alone
choice_b: The U.S. Department of Justice's Antitrust Division
choice_c: The local multiple listing service
choice_d: The National Association of REALTORS
explanation: The DOJ's Antitrust Division has authority to bring criminal prosecutions for Sherman Act violations, while the FTC and private plaintiffs (along with state attorneys general) pursue civil enforcement.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: The "state action" immunity doctrine can shield certain anticompetitive conduct from federal antitrust liability, but this immunity generally requires that the restraint be:
choice_a: Approved informally by a majority of local brokers
choice_b: Consistent with MLS bylaws
choice_c: Clearly articulated as state policy and actively supervised by the state itself -- private real estate industry conduct is not automatically immune merely because the industry is state-licensed
choice_d: Automatically granted to any state-licensed profession
explanation: State action immunity is narrow: it requires that the state clearly articulate the restraint as its own policy and actively supervise its implementation. The mere fact that real estate brokers are state-licensed does not, by itself, immunize private anticompetitive agreements among them.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: A seller signs an exclusive right-to-sell listing agreement with a single brokerage firm, agreeing not to list the property with any other firm during the listing term. Under federal antitrust law, this ordinary exclusive listing arrangement is:
choice_a: A per se illegal group boycott
choice_b: An illegal tying arrangement in all cases
choice_c: A per se illegal market-allocation agreement
choice_d: A lawful vertical agreement between the firm and its own client, not a horizontal restraint among competing firms
explanation: An exclusive listing agreement is a routine vertical arrangement between a brokerage and its own client, not an agreement among competing firms -- so it does not raise the same per se horizontal-restraint concerns as price fixing, boycotts, or market allocation among competitors.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: MLS rules that require participating brokers to cooperate in showing each other's listings are generally lawful and procompetitive. However, such rules can raise antitrust concerns if they:
choice_a: Are used as a vehicle to fix compensation levels, or to exclude or disadvantage certain categories of firms such as discount or limited-service brokerages
choice_b: Simply require accurate property data entry
choice_c: Set standard deadlines for submitting listings
choice_d: Require licensees to be members of the local association to access the database
explanation: Cooperative MLS access rules are generally procompetitive, but they cross into antitrust risk when used to fix or standardize compensation, or to exclude or penalize particular business models (such as discount or limited-service brokers) rather than to serve a legitimate cooperative purpose.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: A group of competing local brokers agrees among themselves to deny MLS access to a new virtual or discount brokerage entering the market, specifically because of its low-fee business model. This coordinated denial of access is best characterized as:
choice_a: A legitimate quality-control measure
choice_b: A group boycott, which can be a per se Sherman Act Section 1 violation when it is the product of an agreement among competitors
choice_c: Outside the scope of federal antitrust law because MLS membership is voluntary
choice_d: A lawful exercise of each broker's individual business judgment
explanation: When competing firms collectively agree to exclude a competitor because of its business model or pricing, that concerted refusal to deal is a group boycott and can be a per se antitrust violation, regardless of MLS membership being nominally voluntary.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: A brokerage publicly announces a new, higher standard commission rate through a press release, apparently inviting competitors to match it, without any direct communication or explicit agreement with those competitors. This kind of public price signaling:
choice_a: Can never raise any antitrust concern because there is no direct communication between competitors
choice_b: Is required by federal law before any commission change
choice_c: Can still draw antitrust scrutiny in some circumstances, because signaling conduct intended to facilitate coordinated pricing may raise concerns even without a formal, provable agreement
choice_d: Only matters if a written contract exists between the firms
explanation: While a unilateral announcement alone does not automatically prove a Section 1 conspiracy, signaling conduct designed to invite or facilitate parallel pricing by competitors can still draw regulatory scrutiny, particularly when paired with other circumstantial evidence suggesting an understanding among competitors.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: Under the "essential facilities" concept sometimes invoked in antitrust disputes involving a dominant local MLS, a claim can arise where:
choice_a: Any two MLS systems exist in neighboring counties
choice_b: A broker simply chooses not to join a particular MLS
choice_c: An MLS charges a reasonable, uniformly applied membership fee to all participants
choice_d: A dominant MLS controls access to a resource that competitors realistically cannot duplicate and then denies access on discriminatory or anticompetitive terms
explanation: The essential facilities theory can apply where a dominant, non-duplicable resource -- such as the primary local MLS database -- is controlled by a party who denies access to competitors on unreasonable or discriminatory terms, potentially raising Section 2 concerns.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: The Clayton Act, in addition to providing a private treble-damages remedy, also addresses mergers and acquisitions. Under Clayton Act Section 7, a merger between two competing real estate brokerage firms could be challenged if it would:
choice_a: Substantially lessen competition or tend to create a monopoly in the relevant market
choice_b: Reduce the number of licensed agents in a state by even one
choice_c: Change the combined firm's name
choice_d: Occur in a state with fewer than one million residents
explanation: Clayton Act Section 7 prohibits mergers and acquisitions whose effect may be to substantially lessen competition or tend to create a monopoly -- a standard that can apply to brokerage consolidation in a sufficiently concentrated local market.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust); Clayton Act Section 7

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: A private plaintiff wishing to bring a civil antitrust claim for treble damages under the Clayton Act arising from a real estate price-fixing conspiracy generally must file suit within:
choice_a: 30 days of discovering the conduct
choice_b: Four years from when the claim accrued, the standard federal statute of limitations for private Clayton Act damages claims
choice_c: There is no time limit for antitrust claims
choice_d: One year, matching most state tort claims
explanation: Private antitrust damages actions under the Clayton Act are generally subject to a four-year statute of limitations, running from when the cause of action accrues (subject to tolling doctrines in some circumstances, such as fraudulent concealment).
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust); Clayton Act limitations period

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: For a per se Sherman Act Section 1 violation such as price fixing among competing brokers, a plaintiff or prosecutor generally does NOT need to separately prove that the conduct:
choice_a: Involved two or more separate competing firms
choice_b: Related to price, output, boycotts, or market division
choice_c: Actually produced anticompetitive effects in the market -- proof of the type of agreement itself is sufficient under the per se rule
choice_d: Occurred at all
explanation: The whole point of per se treatment is that certain categories of restraint -- like naked price fixing among competitors -- are conclusively presumed unreasonable, so no separate showing of actual market harm or anticompetitive effect is required once the agreement itself is proven.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: In a successful private antitrust suit under the Clayton Act, a real estate consumer's actual proven damages of $30,000 from a price-fixing conspiracy among brokers would typically be trebled to:
explanation: "Treble damages" means the plaintiff's proven actual damages are multiplied by three, so $30,000 in actual damages becomes $90,000 in recoverable damages under the Clayton Act's private right of action.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust); Clayton Act private right of action

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: Several unrelated brokerage firms in the same market independently, without any communication or agreement among them, each happen to raise their commission rates around the same time in response to the same rising market conditions. This kind of "conscious parallelism":
choice_a: Does not, by itself, establish an unlawful Section 1 conspiracy -- parallel conduct alone is not proof of an agreement absent additional evidence of coordination
choice_b: Is automatically a per se Sherman Act Section 1 violation
choice_c: Requires no further analysis because parallel pricing is conclusive proof of a conspiracy
choice_d: Is illegal only in real estate and no other industry
explanation: Merely acting similarly to competitors -- consciously observing and reacting to market conditions the same way -- is not itself proof of an unlawful agreement. Section 1 liability requires evidence of actual coordination or communication beyond mere parallel behavior.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust)

topic: Federal Antitrust Law in Real Estate Brokerage
question: A local trade association's bylaws state that member firms may not cooperate on transactions with any non-member brokerage in the area. A group of competing member firms adopts and enforces this rule against non-members. This practice raises antitrust concern primarily because it may function as:
choice_a: A legitimate membership eligibility requirement with no competitive impact
choice_b: A group boycott that excludes non-member competitors from the market through concerted action
choice_c: A tying arrangement between two unrelated products
choice_d: Protected free speech with no antitrust implications
explanation: An association-wide agreement among competing member firms to refuse dealings with non-members can function as a group boycott, using coordinated exclusion to disadvantage outside competitors rather than serving a legitimate, competitively neutral membership purpose.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (antitrust)
